newsitem.title: JAPAN: It's festive at Japan-N.Korea "Checkpoint Charlie".
newsitem.headline: It's festive at Japan-N.Korea "Checkpoint Charlie".

text.p: This is not Checkpoint Charlie.
But every couple of weeks this port on Japan's west coast offers the capitalist west a fleeting glimpse into North Korea, the world's last Stalinist state.

On Monday, as smartly dressed passengers disembarked from the North Korean ferry Mangyongbong 92, it was hard to believe they had just been to a nation portrayed as fighting for survival from a near-famine and dramatic political upheaval.
If the mood was often grim at Checkpoint Charlie, crossing point between West and East Berlin at the height of the Cold War, the scene at this meeting of two worlds was festive.
A 27-year-old man with a golf club practised his chip shot while awaiting the arrival of his girlfriend on the ferry.
As the 9,000-tonne ship hove into sight, the North Korean flag was unfurled on a waiting mini-van and music blared from a loudspeaker.
Passengers, including this time the elegant beauties of the Korea Art Troupe, singers and dancers from Japan, waved from the decks to loved ones waiting on the dock below.
They casually filed off the ferry like British weekend tourists after crossing the English Channel from France.
The only difference was that they carried not wine or cheese but packets of ginseng and bottles of a grain liquor called soju, each with a real dead snake dangling inside.
This time there was a host of reporters waiting for them.

The passengers, all Japanese ethnic Koreans with relatives in North Korea, were possibly the first foreign travel group to return from the secretive communist nation since its ideology chief defected to hated rival South Korea two weeks ago. Then came two other big political shocks in quick succession -- the country's premier was removed and the defence minister died.
The passengers, who have spent the past two weeks in North Korea, mainly the capital Pyongyang, said they saw no sign of turmoil or starvation and their relaxed behaviour backed up their words.

The ferry scene is repeated about twice a month in one of the many contradictions about relations between Japan and North Korea -- two nations which have never had diplomatic relations, regularly denounce each other and yet keep this sea route of contact open.
The ferry plies between Niigata on Japan's western coast and the North Korean port of Wonsan on a voyage that takes about 28 hours.
On the ferry, named after the village where North Korea's dead founder Kim Il-sung was born, there are even bigger contradictions.
A giant portrait of Kim and his son Kim Jong-il, the country's present de facto leader, looks down on a lounge where a vending machine dispenses the modern-day symbol of capitalism -- Coca Cola.

Two Reuter correspondents chosen from waiting journalists for a rare tour by westerners of the ship, technically North Korean territory, met only smiles when they came upon surprised North Korean crew, both men and women.
"We are tired of sinister tales about what goes on here on the ferry," an official who represents North Korea in Japan said in explaining why the tour was allowed.
"See, there are no guns. No secret communications equipment."

The tour appeared part of an effort by North Korea, including a report by official Pyongyang Radio on Saturday of "Dear Leader" Kim's first appearance in three weeks, to show that it was business as usual despite the past days of political turmoil.
